--- Page 1 ---
Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based
Mathematical Optimization Modeling
Ryoichi Takase1
Xian Yeow Lee1
Hikaru Tomonari2
Masaya Tsunokake2
1Hitachi America, Ltd., California, USA
2Hitachi, Ltd., Tokyo, Japan
{ryoichi.takase, xian.lee}@hal.hitachi.com
{hikaru.tomonari.oj, masaya.tsunokake.qu}@hitachi.com
Abstract
Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization mod-
eling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored
for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in
end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible,
or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-
based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components:
mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing
datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different
components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of
failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Further-
more, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible
but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining
gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations
of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture
constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.
1
Introduction
Optimization is central to industrial operations, where planning and scheduling tasks must satisfy
complex constraints arising from safety requirements and regulatory compliance. Optimization
frameworks such as linear programming (LP) and mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) remain
fundamental for achieving efficient and reliable solutions in industrial applications [14, 6]. Meanwhile,
constructing such models typically requires domain expertise and manual effort, limiting scalability
and adaptability to new operational scenarios.
Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has motivated efforts to automatically generate
optimization models from natural-language descriptions [10, 15, 13]. While these approaches demon-
strate promising results, achieving high reliability in industrial-scale problems remains challenging.
In practice, LLM-based optimization systems often fail in multiple ways, including generating non-
executable solver code, producing infeasible formulations, or yielding feasible but incorrect solutions.
Existing work has primarily focused on improving modeling accuracy, with limited attention to
analyzing failure modes in LLM-generated outputs.
In this work, we analyze failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling. We decompose
the modeling process into three components—mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain
knowledge—and construct datasets that explicitly capture each component. Using these datasets, we
examine how different data elements relate to errors in end-to-end generation. Our analysis shows
that different components are associated with distinct failure types, such as non-executable code and
infeasible formulations. While integrating these components improves execution reliability, it does
Preprint.
arXiv:2611.33351v1  [cs.LG]  24 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
not substantially reduce feasible but incorrect solutions, which remain the dominant failure mode
across benchmarks, suggesting a gap between executability and correctness.
2
Method
2.1
End-to-End Optimization Modeling
We define an end-to-end pipeline that maps natural-language descriptions to optimization solutions.
The LLM generates solver-compatible code, which is then executed by a solver to obtain a solution.
The LLM is responsible for (i) translating problem descriptions into mathematical formulations,
(ii) implementing these formulations as executable solver code, and (iii) incorporating domain-
specific constraints required for realistic settings. Errors may arise from multiple sources, including
formulation and solver implementation, and are often entangled in the generated code, making it
difficult to produce correct solutions.
2.2
Decomposing Optimization Modeling into Core Components
Building on the role of LLM in end-to-end optimization modeling, we decompose the process into
three key elements that define distinct aspects of the dataset:
• Mathematical reasoning: Translating real-world requirements into optimization models
involves a structured derivation from informal specifications to decision variables, objective
functions, and constraints. Data that captures such reasoning processes enables models to
learn how to construct well-formed mathematical representations.
• Solver usage: Constructing executable optimization models requires knowledge of solver-
specific APIs and configuration details (e.g., variable types, linearity constraints, and syntax)
as in PySCIPOpt [8]. Data reflecting solver interaction—including both correct usage and
common implementation errors—supports the generation of executable and debuggable
code.
• Domain knowledge: Realistic optimization problems depend on domain-specific constraints
and operational rules. Data incorporating such knowledge defines feasible regions and
dependencies, helping prevent invalid modeling assumptions and improving solution validity.
These elements are tightly coupled, and their interactions may give rise to distinct failure modes. This
design allows us to examine how different aspects of the dataset relate to execution reliability and
solution correctness. We hypothesize that each component is associated with specific failure modes
and that its coverage may influence overall model reliability.
2.3
Constructing Datasets via LLM and Solver Feedback
Figure 1 provides an overview of the data generation pipeline. Datasets are constructed using an LLM-
driven framework that generates optimization modeling tasks through prompting and solver-based
feedback. Math-Opt Reasoning data are generated by prompting the LLM to produce optimization
problems in the form of natural-language descriptions, mathematical formulations, and solver code,
followed by solver-based filtering to retain only solvable instances. Solver Usage data are constructed
by applying iterative debugging to non-executable outputs using error messages and code correction
prompts, capturing common issues in implementation and solver execution. Domain Knowledge
data are obtained by refining infeasible problems with domain-specific constraints and expanding
them through iterative scaling, resulting in more realistic and complex optimization tasks.
In this study, we use gpt-oss-120b [1] as the data-generating LLM and the s1-1.1 dataset [9] as the
starting point for data construction. This process yields three datasets—Math-Opt Reasoning (32K
samples), Solver Usage (4K samples), and Domain Knowledge (8K samples). For each dataset,
5%–8% of samples are reserved for testing and the remainder for training and validation.

3
Results
3.1
Dataset Characteristics and Failure Analysis
To enable comparison of how different datasets capture distinct aspects of optimization modeling,
we examine the model responses using off-the-shelf LLMs (gpt-oss 120B/20B and Qwen3 32B/8B).
These models are used only as diagnostic tools to reveal dataset properties, and the reported metrics
are not intended as model performance benchmarks. In Figures 2 and 3, the Math-Opt Reasoning,
Solver Usage, and Domain Knowledge datasets are shown in red, blue, and orange, respectively,
while existing benchmarks such as ComplexOR [15], IndustryOR [4], and ComplexLP [5] are shown
in grayscale.
As shown in Figure 2, the Math-Opt Reasoning dataset has reasoning lengths comparable to existing
benchmarks. Solver Usage shows similar lengths but lower accuracy, indicating challenges in
generating valid solver code. Domain Knowledge requires more reasoning tokens yet achieves
lower accuracy, reflecting the complexity of incorporating domain-specific constraints. These results
suggest that dataset difficulty depends not only on reasoning length but also on solver requirements
and constraint complexity.
Figure 3 compares non-executable and infeasible rates, revealing distinct failure modes. Solver Usage
has the highest non-executable rate, while Domain Knowledge produces more infeasible solutions
due to complex constraints. In contrast, Math-Opt Reasoning shows error rates comparable to existing
benchmarks. Overall, non-executable errors and infeasibility arise from different sources, reflecting
distinct challenges in optimization modeling.
Figure 2: Modeling accuracy and reasoning-token usage. The Math-Opt Reasoning dataset requires
reasoning tokens comparable to existing benchmarks, while Solver Usage achieves lower accu-
racy with similar token lengths. Domain Knowledge requires more tokens due to domain-specific
formulation complexity.
3


--- Page 4 ---
Figure 3: Non-executable and infeasible rates. Math-Opt Reasoning shows error rates comparable to
existing benchmarks, while Solver Usage has higher non-executable rates and Domain Knowledge
higher infeasible rates, highlighting distinct challenges.
Figure 4: Failure patterns across benchmarks: although the non-executable rate decreases with
fine-tuning, LLMs still produce wrong objectives (i.e., feasible but incorrect solutions), particularly
in more complex tasks.
3.2
Effect and Limitations of Data Components
To analyze the contribution of each data component, we fine-tune LLMs on the constructed datasets
and perform ablation studies by removing reasoning, solver usage, or domain knowledge. We
evaluate models on standard benchmarks (ComplexOR, IndustryOR, ComplexLP, NLP4LP, NL4Opt),
categorizing outputs into five types: non-executable, timeout, infeasible, feasible but incorrect, and
correct. To account for stochasticity, we sample multiple outputs per instance (32 for ComplexOR
and 4 for others) and report averaged results.
Experiments on Qwen3 models (1.7B and 4B) [16], using teacher data generated from a Qwen3-32B
model via solver-based rejection sampling, show that the full dataset consistently yields the best
performance (Tables 1 and 2), suggesting that all components are beneficial. Removing solver usage
data increases non-executable outputs, although the causal relationship remains unclear.
Nevertheless, across all settings, including larger 32B models fine-tuned with GRPO [11], feasible but
incorrect outputs (denoted as Wrong Obj.) remain dominant (Figure 4). Although fine-tuning reduces
non-executable errors, this failure mode persists and becomes more pronounced as task complexity
increases, indicating that LLMs often generate plausible yet invalid optimization formulations.
Our results reveal a key limitation of current LLM-based optimization systems: while data-centric
design reduces explicit failures such as non-executable outputs, it does not adequately address formu-
lation errors. In particular, feasible but incorrect solutions remain dominant, often caused by subtle
issues such as missing constraints or incorrect objectives that are difficult to detect through standard
supervision or execution-based validation. This suggests that improving reliability requires datasets
that explicitly capture formulation structure, constraint completeness, and boundary conditions,
enabling models to distinguish correct formulations from near-correct ones.
4


--- Page 5 ---
4
Conclusion
This work presents an analysis of failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling. We show that
different data components correspond to distinct failure modes and that integrating them improves
execution reliability. However, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode,
highlighting a gap between executability and correctness. Addressing this limitation requires new
dataset designs that better capture the structure of valid optimization formulations and reduce such
errors in end-to-end pipelines.

A
Method Details
A.1
Three Key Elements in Mathematical Optimization
Formulating real-world problems as solvable optimization models requires integrating three key
elements to ensure correctness and practical feasibility.
• Mathematical reasoning: Transforming real-world requirements into optimization models
requires a logical, step-by-step derivation from informal specifications to decision variables,
objectives, and constraints. This reasoning ensures that optimization models capture the
essential structure of the problem and yield well-defined mathematical formulations.
• Solver usage: Implementing optimization models correctly requires familiarity with solver-
specific APIs and parameters (e.g., variable types and linearity/convexity requirements) as
in Gurobi [3] and PySCIPOpt [8]. Understanding syntax, configuration, and debugging is
essential for producing executable, solver-ready code.
• Domain knowledge: Background knowledge of operational rules and industry constraints
in OT domains helps define the feasible decision space and its dependencies, thereby pre-
venting invalid modeling assumptions and ensuring that optimization formulations maintain
correctness and practical feasibility.
Motivated by the importance of combining mathematical reasoning, appropriate solver usage, and
industry-specific domain knowledge, we propose a data-generation method that integrates these three
elements to train LLMs to produce solvable optimization models. As shown in Figure 1, our pipeline
unifies these key components, which are described in detail below.
A.2
Step 1: Data Generation Based on Mathematical Reasoning
This data-generation step extracts multi-step reasoning traces from mathematical reasoning datasets
and converts them into optimization modeling tasks covering a wide range of domains and problem
types. Solver-based filtering retains only solvable problems that require both reasoning and modeling
skills.
Math2Opt first prompts an LLM to generate a multi-step reasoning trace from a math problem
and its solution, and then converts this trace into a new mathematical optimization problem. The
prompt instructs the LLM to construct an optimization model whose variables, constraints, and
objective are derived from the reasoning steps. The resulting data consists of three components:
(i) a natural-language problem description, (ii) a mathematical formulation, and (iii) PySCIPOpt
code. This process ensures that the generated data imposes multi-step reasoning on LLMs rather than
simple text-to-equation conversion.
Domain Change increases dataset diversity by mapping each seed optimization problem to one
of 18 application domains (e.g., manufacturing, supply chain, energy), following [2, 7]. For each
seed problem, an LLM generates a new version in a specified target domain while preserving the
structural pattern of the original formulation. By systematically creating domain-specific variations,
this process enhances cross-domain reasoning in LLMs.
Problem Type Change further increases dataset diversity by introducing multiple classes of opti-
mization problems, including Linear Programming (LP), Nonlinear Programming (NLP), Quadratic
Programming (QP), and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). Similar to the previous step, the
LLM reformulates each seed problem into a new problem belonging to one of these classes, enabling
LLMs to deal with a wide range of objectives and constraints.
Solver & Filtering validates the generated problems by executing solvers and retaining only those that
yield optimal solutions. These filtered samples constitute the Math-Opt Reasoning Data. Samples
that fail to solve are used for subsequent steps.
A.3
Step 2: Data Generation for Solver Usage from Non-Executable Data
Among the failed samples from Step 1, we categorize the errors as follows:
• Infeasible: No solution exists under the given objectives and constraints.
6


--- Page 7 ---
• Timeout: Computation could not be completed within the specified time limit.
• Non-executable: Solver execution failed due to errors.
Infeasible samples typically require substantial reformulation of the objectives or constraints and are
therefore used in Step 3, which leverages domain knowledge. Timeout samples constitute only a
small fraction of failures and are excluded from data generation.
In Step 2, we focus on non-executable samples and debug them to extract the cases from which the
correct solver code can be successfully recovered. These samples are typically resolved by fixing code
or configuration errors, and the resulting corrections provide valuable information on the appropriate
problem formulations.
Code Debugging is applied to non-executable code in representative OT domains, such as man-
ufacturing, supply chain, and energy, to reduce data construction time. These domains provide
diverse formulations and solver usage, ensuring sufficient dataset coverage. A debugging prompt
is constructed by combining the problem description, source code, and associated error messages,
and is then provided to the LLM. By resolving common errors that prevent successful execution,
this process yields datasets that help LLMs learn the correct optimization formulation and solver
configuration. Only code that becomes executable after several debugging iterations is reserved as
Solver Usage Data. Samples that remain non-executable or result in timeouts after the debugging
iterations are discarded, whereas infeasible samples are used in Step 3.
A.4
Step 3: Data Generation Leveraging Domain Knowledge Using Infeasible Data
In real-world optimization problems, operational rules and requirements often introduce complex
constraints that can produce infeasible solutions. In Step 3, the infeasible samples obtained from
the previous steps are iteratively analyzed and corrected, thus ensuring the validity of the resulting
dataset. Furthermore, by scaling the problem size, we construct more domain-aware optimization
problems that integrate relevant expert knowledge.
Infeasibility Debugging refines infeasible samples by prompting the LLM to determine whether the
infeasibility arises from a coding error or a modeling issue, then minimally reformulates the problem
and updates the code while preserving intent. By making only minimal changes to restore feasibility,
the method produces samples near the feasible–infeasible boundary.
Solution Validity Debugging constructs a prompt from the problem description, code, and solver
output to obtain relevant domain knowledge from the LLM1. This domain knowledge is then used
to revise the objective and constraints, so the optimization model yields realistic solutions. During
iteration, samples that time out or become non-executable are processed again to obtain feasible
solutions, while samples that become infeasible are handled with infeasibility debugging. In the end,
this process produces the Domain Knowledge Seed Data, which serve as starting points for scaling
the optimization problem.
Problem Scaling expands the Domain Knowledge Seed Data by applying one of the three types of
domain knowledge, such as insights, operational rules, or tacit knowledge. Each type is used to
introduce additional decision variables or constraints. For example, when leveraging operational
rules, we scale the problem by adding new decision variables in the target OT domain using the
following prompt: “In particular, incorporate key operational rules from the energy domain, increase
the number of decision variables, and significantly expand the problem scale”2.
After an optimal solution is found under the initial scaling, additional scaling is applied to further
expand the problem. If this scaling results in timeouts or non-executable samples, the previous scaling
level is retried to obtain an optimal solution. When infeasibility arises, infeasibility debugging with
domain knowledge is applied. Samples that yield optimal solutions after this process are reserved as
Domain Knowledge Scaled Data.
1In this study, domain knowledge refers to short, listed statements describing physical or operational rules that are generated
by the LLM. For example, in the energy domain, the generated list includes statements on charger efficiency, grid peak-demand
limits, and tariff constraints.
2Examples of added operational rules include required shut-down periods for thermal protection and associated start-up
cost effects.

Figure 5: Overview of training reasoning LLMs. Left: Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT), which
generates multiple reasoning traces using Math-Opt Reasoning Data, Solver Usage Data, and Domain
Knowledge Seed Data, using only solver-verified correct traces for training. Right: Reinforcement
Learning (RL), which trains the model on Solver Usage Data and Domain Knowledge Scaled Data,
with solver-executed reasoning traces providing binary rewards based on objective value correctness.
In the proposed method, we used the gpt-oss-120b [1] as the data-generating LLM and the s1-1.1
dataset [9] as the starting point for mathematical reasoning data, from which we produced four
datasets: Math-Opt Reasoning Data (31,773 samples), Solver Usage Data (4,264 samples), Domain
Knowledge Seed Data (735 samples), and Domain Knowledge Scaled Data (7,009 samples). For
each dataset, approximately 5% to 8% of the samples were reserved as test data, while the remaining
samples were used for training and validation purposes.
A.5
Training Reasoning LLMs
In this study, we adopt Qwen3-32B [16] as the base reasoning model. Our dataset contains the
problem description, code, and ground-truth objective value, but does not include the reasoning traces
required for training. To obtain these traces, we apply Qwen3-32B to our dataset and generate the
corresponding reasoning traces. As shown in Figure 5, we first apply Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning
(RFT) to improve the accuracy of mathematical optimization modeling, followed by reinforcement
learning (RL) to further enhance overall performance.
Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT)
We construct training data using Math-Opt Reasoning Data, Solver Usage Data, and Domain Knowl-
edge Seed Data. For each problem, we sample 8 reasoning traces from the Math-Opt Reasoning Data
and 16 reasoning paths from the Solver Usage Data and Domain Knowledge Seed Data. We then
execute a solver on the sampled reasoning paths and extract only those whose objective values match
the ground-truth results, thereby producing three types of RFT data: Math-Opt Reasoning RFT Data
(57,025 samples), Solver Usage RFT Data (1,477 samples), and Domain Knowledge Seed RFT Data
(946 samples)3.
For the Math-Opt Reasoning Data, we additionally perform debugging, and any correctly solved
samples are incorporated into the Debugging RFT Data (24,253 samples). In contrast, debugging
is not performed for the Solver Usage Data or the Domain Knowledge Seed Data, as these will be
repeatedly evaluated later through RL.
3Solver Usage Data and Domain Knowledge Seed Data are more difficult than Math-Opt Reasoning Data. The pass rates
for Math-Opt Reasoning Data, Solver Usage Data, and Domain Knowledge Seed Data are 0.27, 0.051, and 0.17, respectively.
In addition, RFT for Solver Usage Data and Domain Knowledge Seed Data use only subsets that are not included in RL
training, resulting in fewer correct samples compared to Math-Opt Reasoning Data.

Reinforcement Learning (RL)
We perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [11] using the Solver Usage Data and the
Domain Knowledge Scaled Data. To compute the reward, we first extract the code from the reasoning
traces generated by the LLM, and then execute a solver on the extracted code to obtain its objective
value. We assign a reward of 1 if the resulting objective value matches the ground-truth value, and
0 otherwise. This reward function is designed to directly reflect optimization-modeling quality by
evaluating the accuracy of the objective values. The LLM parameters are then updated to maximize
this reward, thereby improving the LLM’s mathematical optimization modeling capability. In this
study, we set the sampling parameters to temperature = 0.6, TopK = 20, and TopP = 0.95. For each
problem, four reasoning trajectories were generated. The RL training is performed using verl [12].
B
Additional Results
B.1
Ablation Study on Small Models
To verify that integrating mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge leads to
improved performance, we conduct an ablation study with four settings: using all three components,
removing Math-Opt Reasoning data, removing Solver Usage data, and removing Domain Knowledge
data. Each dataset remains identical across configurations, and the total number of training steps
and the overall amount of data used to update the LLM are kept constant across all four cases. We
conducted the ablations on the 1.7B and 4B models due to the computational cost of 32B-scale
experiments, while maintaining sensitivity to performance differences. The results are shown in
Tables 1 and 2. The Full setting achieves the best overall performance, indicating that combining
all three forms of supervision is crucial. Although further analysis is needed to quantify each
component’s contribution, the consistent trend across both the 1.7B and 4B models supports the
benefit of integrating mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge.
B.2
Reasoning LLM Training Results
For performance evaluation, we adopted five benchmark datasets: ComplexOR [15], IndustryOR [4],
NL4Opt [10], NLP4LP [2], and ComplexLP [5], which are widely used in optimization modeling
research [13]. To ensure the robustness of the results, we employed a multi-sampling strategy.
Specifically, for the ComplexOR dataset, 32 candidate solutions were sampled for each problem due
to the small amout of data size, while for the remaining datasets, four candidate solutions per problem
were generated. The final accuracy was computed as the average across all sampled solutions. This
approach mitigates variance caused by stochastic generation and provides a more reliable estimate of
model performance.
9


--- Page 10 ---
Table 3 shows the training results. Supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning consistently
improve optimization-modeling performance over the base model, and the 32B model reaches
performance comparable to or exceeding o3 on several benchmarks. However, the key observation is
that improved benchmark performance does not fully resolve the reliability challenges of optimization
modeling. The dominant remaining failure mode is feasible but incorrect solutions, indicating that
many generated formulations can be executed successfully while still encoding incorrect objectives
or constraints. This finding highlights the importance of datasets and training signals that emphasize
formulation correctness in addition to executability.
